scenarios.title: Build a dependable short-option report
scenarios.summary: Accept different option spellings without damaging the evidence.
scenarios.objective:
Build a report command. Before the single SOURCE operand, accept -q (omit the Tag line), -n TAG (default incident) and -o FILE (write the report there instead of stdout). Options may be reordered, repeated or clustered; required values may be attached or separate. The last -n or -o wins. An exact -- ends options; stop scanning at the first operand. A value required by -n may itself be --. TAG and any chosen output name must be nonempty.

Require exactly one existing SOURCE. On success return 0 with no errors: normally print Tag: TAG and a line break, then the exact SOURCE bytes; with -q print only those bytes. With -o, only that output may change and stdout is empty. Never overwrite SOURCE or keep.txt. Any unknown option, missing value, bad operand count, absent source or forbidden/empty output prints Usage: report [-q] [-n TAG] [-o FILE] SOURCE and a line break only to standard error, returns 2 and changes no file. Values are one-line text; filenames follow the supplied flat-name format. Use the supplied filenames exactly.

initial.source: # Build the complete interface and preserve the supplied files.

cases.name: Default report
cases.stdout:
Tag: incident
Rack check
Power ready

after./work/plan.txt:
Tag: Night desk
Rack check
Power ready

cases.name: Repeated name last value wins
cases.stdout:
Tag: second
Rack check
Power ready

solution:
usage() { printf 'Usage: report [-q] [-n TAG] [-o FILE] SOURCE\n' >&2; }
tag=incident
quiet=no
writing=no
destination=
while getopts ':qn:o:' option; do
    case "$option" in
        q) quiet=yes ;;
        n) tag=$OPTARG ;;
        o) destination=$OPTARG; writing=yes ;;
        ?|:) usage; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$tag"; then
    usage; exit 2
fi
if test -f "$1"; then
    source=$1
else
    usage; exit 2
fi
if test "$writing" = yes; then
    if test -z "$destination" || test "$destination" = "$source" || test "$destination" = keep.txt; then
        usage; exit 2
    fi
    if test "$quiet" = yes; then
        cat "$source" > "$destination"
    else
        printf 'Tag: %s\n' "$tag" > "$destination"
        cat "$source" >> "$destination"
    fi
else
    if test "$quiet" = no; then printf 'Tag: %s\n' "$tag"; fi
    cat "$source"
fi

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use argument checks from “Build a reliable report-mode interface”, shift from “Separate a header from the remaining items” and fixed-format printing. This lesson introduces getopts.

concepts.title: Read one option at a time
concepts.text: while getopts ":sn:" choice; do ...; done calls the builtin repeatedly while its status is 0. The declaration lists s as a flag and n: as an option requiring a value. Each success stores s or n in choice. OPTARG holds the required value. In an assignment such as label=$OPTARG it stays one value; quote it when passing it onward.

concepts.title: An option word is not always one option
concepts.text: -snWest is the flag -s followed by -n with value West. -sn West consumes the next argument instead. Repeated flags are allowed. An option-looking required value, even --, is data. A plain operand stops scanning; options are not moved past it. An exact -- encountered as an option ends the loop.

concepts.title: Check errors, then find the operands
concepts.text: The leading : suppresses automatic diagnostics. In the case body use ?|:) for an unknown option or missing required value; print your own message and exit 2. Normal end returns 1. shift "$((OPTIND - 1))" removes just the consumed option arguments; now $1 is the first operand. Validate the remaining count and values before any output redirection.

concepts.title: Keep interface policy separate from scanning
concepts.text: getopts does not decide defaults, nonempty values or whether a destination may replace a source. Those are your task rules. Set defaults before the loop; assign a required value when its option appears so the final occurrence wins. Do all checks before opening an output file.

teaching.example:
label=museum
short=no
while getopts ':sn:' choice; do
    case "$choice" in
        s) short=yes ;;
        n) label=$OPTARG ;;
        ?|:) printf 'Need loan options and TITLE\n' >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$label"; then
    printf 'Need loan options and TITLE\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
printf 'Loan: %s\n' "$1"
if test "$short" = no; then printf 'Shelf: %s\n' "$label"; fi
teaching.inputs: Museum arguments are -sn, East wing and Map set. The separate museum file stays unchanged. The example uses -s and -n; the assignment has its own -q/-n/-o report interface.
teaching.try_change: In the s) arm change short=yes to short=no and Run. The same options now display the Shelf line too. Restore short=yes to repair the example.

scenarios.title: Keep repeated export jobs independent
scenarios.summary: Reuse one parser without leaking a previous job’s options or defaults.
scenarios.objective:
Two script arguments name existing job files. Job files are argument lists, not shell scripts: one line is exactly one argument. A blank line is an empty argument; spaces inside a line stay together. Supplied lines have no leading/trailing space or tab and no embedded line break; the final line may lack its ending line break. Quotes and backslashes are literal data, not quoting syntax. Read with read -r and store each line in a quoted array element. Do not split on spaces, evaluate the file or change IFS. Each job accepts -s (short form), -p PREFIX (default export), then exactly one nonempty LABEL. Support option order, clusters, attached/separate values and --; stop at the first operand. The final -p wins, and PREFIX must be nonempty.

Process both jobs independently in argument order, even after one fails. A valid job prints Job N: Export LABEL using PREFIX and a line break, or Job N: PREFIX:LABEL with -s. A bad option/value/label or extra operand prints only Rejected job N and a line break to standard error for that job. After both, print Defaults: DEFAULT and a line break using the original supplied DEFAULT value. Return 0 if both jobs succeed, otherwise 1. Preserve every file. If there are not exactly two nonempty existing filenames, print only Need two job files and a line break to standard error, return 2 and process neither. Use the supplied filenames exactly.

solution:
describe() {
    local OPTIND=1
    local option
    local prefix=export
    local short=no
    while getopts ':sp:' option; do
        case "$option" in
            s) short=yes ;;
            p) prefix=$OPTARG ;;
            ?|:) return 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
    if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$prefix"; then return 2; fi
    if test "$short" = yes; then
        description="$prefix:$1"
    else
        description="Export $1 using $prefix"
    fi
}
if test "$#" -ne 2; then printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
if test -z "$1" || test -z "$2"; then printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
if test -f "$1" && test -f "$2"; then
    failed=0
else
    printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
prefix=$DEFAULT
number=0
for file in "$@"; do
    number=$((number + 1))
    arguments=()
    while read -r item || test -n "$item"; do
        arguments=("${arguments[@]}" "$item")
    done < "$file"
    if describe "${arguments[@]}"; then
        printf 'Job %s: %s\n' "$number" "$description"
    else
        printf 'Rejected job %s\n' "$number" >&2
        failed=1
    fi
done
printf 'Defaults: %s\n' "$prefix"
exit "$failed"

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use “Build a dependable short-option report”, “Preview and publish a safe handover”, “Protect the report heading”, “Reject one item without ending the batch” and “Investigate findings without losing their status”. This lesson adds an explicitly local scanner and argument files.

concepts.title: Each function gets its own scan
concepts.text: local and indexed arrays are Bash features. A function receives its own positional arguments, but getopts scanner state is normally shared. Begin a reusable parser with local OPTIND=1. This starts a fresh scan for this call and restores the caller’s scan on return. Use the explicit =1 form here. Merely changing the result variable does not reset the scanner.

concepts.title: Keep defaults local as well
concepts.text: local prefix=export and local short=no give each call its own settings. local option keeps the result name from leaking. shift changes only this function’s remaining arguments. Return 2 for a bad job instead of exit, so the caller can continue with the next one.

concepts.title: A file can store argument boundaries
concepts.text: Job files are argument lists, not shell scripts: one line is exactly one argument. A blank line is an empty argument; spaces inside a line stay together. Supplied lines have no leading/trailing space or tab and no embedded line break; the final line may lack its ending line break. Quotes and backslashes are literal data, not quoting syntax. Read with read -r and store each line in a quoted array element. Do not split on spaces, evaluate the file or change IFS. Start arguments=(). In while read -r item || test -n "$item"; do ...; done < "$file", append with arguments=("${arguments[@]}" "$item"). Rebuilding the dense list preserves empty and spaced arguments. The final test includes an unterminated last line; a final empty read is not an extra argument.

concepts.title: Output and status are separate results
concepts.text: Use if describe "${arguments[@]}"; then ...; else ...; fi. The call receives each stored argument separately. The helper intentionally sets one shared description variable, while keeping its scanner and defaults local. Only use that description after success; return 2 on error before setting it. Print the failure for this job and still run the next.

teaching.example:
describe() {
    local OPTIND=1
    local option
    local prefix=museum
    local short=no
    while getopts ':sp:' option; do
        case "$option" in
            s) short=yes ;;
            p) prefix=$OPTARG ;;
            ?|:) return 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
    if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$prefix"; then return 2; fi
    if test "$short" = yes; then
        description="$prefix:$1"
    else
        description="Loan $1 from $prefix"
    fi
}
if test "$#" -ne 2; then printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
if test -z "$1" || test -z "$2"; then printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2; fi
if test -f "$1" && test -f "$2"; then
    failed=0
else
    printf 'Need two job files\n' >&2; exit 2
fi
prefix=$DEFAULT
number=0
for file in "$@"; do
    number=$((number + 1))
    arguments=()
    while read -r item || test -n "$item"; do
        arguments=("${arguments[@]}" "$item")
    done < "$file"
    if describe "${arguments[@]}"; then
        printf 'Job %s: %s\n' "$number" "$description"
    else
        printf 'Rejected job %s\n' "$number" >&2
        failed=1
    fi
done
printf 'Shelf default: %s\n' "$prefix"
exit "$failed"

scenarios.title: Publish only a fully validated export batch
scenarios.summary: Keep global options, independent job options and final publication separate.
scenarios.objective:
Build a two-level export planner. Global options before the first job filename are -a (apply; default preview) and -o DEST (default plan.txt). Support order, repetition, clusters, attached/separate values and --; the final -o wins. Require one or more existing nonempty job filenames. DEST must be nonempty, different from every supplied job filename and different from keep.txt.

Job files are argument lists, not shell scripts: one line is exactly one argument. A blank line is an empty argument; spaces inside a line stay together. Supplied lines have no leading/trailing space or tab and no embedded line break; the final line may lack its ending line break. Quotes and backslashes are literal data, not quoting syntax. Read with read -r and store each line in a quoted array element. Do not split on spaces, evaluate the file or change IFS. Each job has the same -s/-p PREFIX/LABEL interface as “Keep repeated export jobs independent”: default prefix export, nonempty prefix and exactly one nonempty label, first-operand stopping, clusters, attached/separate values, -- and last -p wins. Parse each job independently after parsing globals.

Validate all globals, filenames and jobs before printing a preview or changing a file. For a valid batch, build one line per job in argument order: Export LABEL using PREFIX, or PREFIX:LABEL with -s. Preview prints Preview: and a line break, then all plan lines, returns 0 and changes no file. Apply replaces only DEST with those plan lines (each ends in a line break), prints Published: COUNT and a line break, and returns 0. All other files remain byte-exact. Any invalid global/job option, missing/empty value, wrong/missing job operand or forbidden destination prints only Invalid batch and a line break to standard error, returns 2, prints no normal output and changes no file. The goal is a two-level parser and all-job preflight, not a shell-command interpreter. Use the supplied filenames exactly.

solution:
describe() {
    local OPTIND=1
    local option
    local prefix=export
    local short=no
    while getopts ':sp:' option; do
        case "$option" in
            s) short=yes ;;
            p) prefix=$OPTARG ;;
            ?|:) return 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
    if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$prefix"; then return 2; fi
    if test "$short" = yes; then
        printf '%s:%s\n' "$prefix" "$1"
    else
        printf 'Export %s using %s\n' "$1" "$prefix"
    fi
}
invalid() { printf 'Invalid batch\n' >&2; }
apply=no
destination=plan.txt
while getopts ':ao:' option; do
    case "$option" in
        a) apply=yes ;;
        o) destination=$OPTARG ;;
        ?|:) invalid; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
if test "$#" -eq 0 || test -z "$destination" || test "$destination" = keep.txt; then invalid; exit 2; fi
for file in "$@"; do
    if test -z "$file" || test "$destination" = "$file"; then invalid; exit 2; fi
    if test -f "$file"; then
        ready=yes
    else
        invalid; exit 2
    fi
done
plan=()
for file in "$@"; do
    arguments=()
    while read -r item || test -n "$item"; do
        arguments=("${arguments[@]}" "$item")
    done < "$file"
    if description=$(describe "${arguments[@]}"); then
        plan=("${plan[@]}" "$description")
    else
        invalid; exit 2
    fi
done
if test "$apply" = yes; then
    printf '' > "$destination"
    for row in "${plan[@]}"; do printf '%s\n' "$row" >> "$destination"; done
    printf 'Published: %s\n' "${#plan[@]}"
else
    printf 'Preview:\n'
    for row in "${plan[@]}"; do printf '%s\n' "$row"; done
fi

teaching.prerequisite_note: Use “Keep repeated export jobs independent”, “Assemble a bundle only after preflight checks” and “Preview or publish a validated release plan”. This task adds outer and per-job option interfaces to the same batch; the job files contain argument boundaries, not commands.

concepts.title: Two interfaces share a scanner unless you separate them
concepts.text: The outer getopts loop parses global -a/-o before filenames. After its shift, the scanner has still already been used. Each job helper therefore needs its own local OPTIND=1; do not reuse the outer index for a job’s argument vector. One job may end normally and another may have a different number of options.

concepts.title: Load arguments, not commands
concepts.text: Job files are argument lists, not shell scripts: one line is exactly one argument. A blank line is an empty argument; spaces inside a line stay together. Supplied lines have no leading/trailing space or tab and no embedded line break; the final line may lack its ending line break. Quotes and backslashes are literal data, not quoting syntax. Read with read -r and store each line in a quoted array element. Do not split on spaces, evaluate the file or change IFS. Reuse the quoted array-loading loop from the preceding lesson. A job’s own -- and required -- value have their own meaning inside that job; they do not change outer global options. Never pass job text to eval or try to split it as a command.

concepts.title: Finish every check before publication
concepts.text: Create plan=(), capture one successful description at a time and retain it with plan=("${plan[@]}" "$description"). If any helper fails, exit before printing the preview header or opening DEST. Once every job passes, loop over the saved descriptions. ${#plan[@]} counts jobs, including repeated source filenames.

concepts.title: Preview and apply have different effects
concepts.text: Preview prints the completed plan and preserves even an old destination. Apply may first clear its validated destination with printf empty text, then append each saved description. Both use the same validated data. No helper should write to the final destination while still checking a job.

teaching.example:
describe() {
    local OPTIND=1
    local option
    local prefix=museum
    local short=no
    while getopts ':sp:' option; do
        case "$option" in
            s) short=yes ;;
            p) prefix=$OPTARG ;;
            ?|:) return 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
    if test "$#" -ne 1 || test -z "$1" || test -z "$prefix"; then return 2; fi
    if test "$short" = yes; then
        printf '%s:%s\n' "$prefix" "$1"
    else
        printf 'Loan %s from %s\n' "$1" "$prefix"
    fi
}
invalid() { printf 'Invalid batch\n' >&2; }
apply=no
destination=docket.txt
while getopts ':ao:' option; do
    case "$option" in
        a) apply=yes ;;
        o) destination=$OPTARG ;;
        ?|:) invalid; exit 2 ;;
    esac
done
shift "$((OPTIND - 1))"
if test "$#" -eq 0 || test -z "$destination" || test "$destination" = "museum keep.txt"; then invalid; exit 2; fi
for file in "$@"; do
    if test -z "$file" || test "$destination" = "$file"; then invalid; exit 2; fi
    if test -f "$file"; then
        ready=yes
    else
        invalid; exit 2
    fi
done
plan=()
for file in "$@"; do
    arguments=()
    while read -r item || test -n "$item"; do
        arguments=("${arguments[@]}" "$item")
    done < "$file"
    if description=$(describe "${arguments[@]}"); then
        plan=("${plan[@]}" "$description")
    else
        invalid; exit 2
    fi
done
if test "$apply" = yes; then
    printf '' > "$destination"
    for row in "${plan[@]}"; do printf '%s\n' "$row" >> "$destination"; done
    printf 'Filed: %s\n' "${#plan[@]}"
else
    printf 'Preview:\n'
    for row in "${plan[@]}"; do printf '%s\n' "$row"; done
fi
teaching.inputs: The example uses maps.args, guides.args, docket.txt and museum keep.txt. The assignment uses different red/blue/bad jobs and protected keep.txt. The example begins in preview and has no global options.
teaching.try_change: Change only the initial apply=no to apply=yes and Run. The complete museum plan now replaces docket.txt and prints Filed: 2; museum keep.txt and both job files stay unchanged. Restore apply=no to return to preview.
